sections.label: Overview
sections.content:
False Creek South represents one of Vancouver's most successful experiments in mixed-tenure community development. Built on former industrial land in the 1970s and 1980s, this approximately 100-acre neighbourhood demonstrates how public land ownership can support diverse housing options while maintaining long-term affordability.

The City of Vancouver owns about 80 acres in False Creek South, making it a rare example of large-scale public land stewardship. The neighbourhood includes a mix of co-op, non-market rental, market rental, and strata leasehold housing, alongside civic and commercial uses.

False Creek South Neighbourhood Association (FCSNA) is the resident neighbourhood association. Its RePlan Committee leads community planning conversations, while the False Creek South Community Housing Trust is a separate organization focused on long-term housing stewardship and affordability.

Robyn Chan, Project Manager for RePlan, the planning committee of the False Creek South Neighbourhood Association, has also supported False Creek South Community Housing Trust outreach with co-op boards and residents. A civic engagement specialist with a Masters in Urban Studies from SFU, Chan has been working with the neighbourhood to connect community planning, resident engagement, and the push for long-term housing affordability.

sections.label: Housing Model
sections.content:
Mixed Tenure Breakdown

False Creek South includes multiple tenure types, each serving different community needs:

  • Co-operatives: City data identifies seven co-op buildings (517 units) on City land, and two are already working with FCS CLT: False Creek Co-op and Alder Bay Co-op. Members have secure tenure and participate in democratic governance.
  • Non-Market Rental: Below-market housing operated by non-profit societies, ensuring affordability for lower-income residents.
  • Market Rental: Rental housing at market rates.
  • Strata Residential: Privately-owned condominiums within the mixed community.
  • City-Owned Properties: Land and buildings retained by the City of Vancouver.
  • Commercial & Civic: Including False Creek School and retail frontages.

The Land Lease Model

Housing operators lease land from the city rather than purchasing it. Most City-land lease terms expire between 2036 and 2046, creating both opportunity and uncertainty. This model:

  • Keeps land costs out of housing prices
  • Prevents speculation and land flipping
  • Maintains public control over development decisions
  • Allows the city to enforce affordability requirements

The Lease Renewal Moment

The original 60-year leases are approaching expiry, creating uncertainty for households across the neighbourhood. In October 2021, Vancouver City Council received a False Creek South landowner update, and in March 2024 Vancouver City Council directed city staff to report back with an updated and enhanced development framework. On January 22, 2025, Vancouver City Council approved entering negotiations with Arup Canada Inc. for consulting services, with an estimated contract value of $4 million.

Community Land Trust Initiative

In March 2024, Vancouver City Council passed a motion supporting community land trust models and the construction of newly built co-op housing on City-owned land. The False Creek South Community Housing Trust received funding from Vancity Community Foundation to develop a business plan and engage with co-op boards. As Robyn Chan explains: "It's a way to have more control and to expand non-profit housing."

Recent grant-funded projects include embodied-carbon research comparing demolition versus lease extensions, described in RePlan's 2024 annual report, and a capacity-building program supporting governance, community engagement, and long-term financial planning.
keyPoints: About 80 acres are on City-owned land
1,849 housing units are on City land, plus 1,354 units on non-City land
Most City-land leases expire in 2036-2046 — a critical transition period
January 22, 2025: Vancouver City Council approved negotiations for a consulting contract valued at up to $4 million
March 2024: Vancouver City Council motion supports community land trust models and new co-op housing on City-owned land

sections.label: Overview
sections.content:
Sen̓áḵw (pronounced "sen-AHK-w") means "the place inside the head of False Creek." It is one of the largest Indigenous-led urban housing developments in Canada. It is being built on 10.5 acres of Squamish Nation reserve land near the south end of the Burrard Bridge.

The project is planned as 6,000+ purpose-built rental homes, including 1,200+ below-market homes. Hiy̓ám̓ Housing, the Squamish Nation housing society, states that 250 homes are allocated for Squamish People through its housing stream.

Phase One includes three towers and 1,409 homes. In its February 5, 2026 update, Squamish Nation said first move-ins were expected in summer 2026, with phase-one homes prioritized for Squamish People.

Sen̓áḵw received $1.4 billion in financial support from CMHC for early phases of the project.

sections.label: Land Rights
sections.content:
Federal Jurisdiction & Public Views

Sen̓áḵw is on federal reserve land. The City of Vancouver states that city land-use policies and regulations do not apply to these lands, and the City is not directly involved in planning or design approvals.

For context, Vancouver's protected public-view framework has been in place since 1989. On July 10, 2024, Council replaced the old View Protection Guidelines with new Public Views Guidelines, including amendments to some public views.

Ownership & Partnership

On August 28, 2025, OPTrust announced it had acquired Westbank's interest in Phases One and Two. OPTrust and the Squamish Nation now each hold 50% ownership in those phases, while Squamish Nation holds 100% ownership of Phases Three and Four.

Services Agreement

The City of Vancouver and Squamish Nation signed a services agreement on May 25, 2022. The Service Agreement Overview states a 120-year term applying to all four phases. It also states that the City provides core municipal services, and the Nation pays annual charges using the same methodology applied to other Vancouver property owners.

The same overview states that the first two phases are expected to include approximately 2,950 rental units, including 590 affordable units (20%), plus 65-75 childcare spaces.

Tenant Protections

In July 2023, Squamish Nation announced that protections in BC's Residential Tenancy Act (BCRTA) would be in place for Sen̓áḵw through the federal First Nations Commercial and Industrial Development Act (FNCIDA). The Squamish Nation Residential Tenancy Regulations (SOR/2023-135) are now in force under FNCIDA.

Indigenous Land Development in BC

BSH's Urban Indigenous Housing in British Columbia research found that although municipalities often express a commitment to reconciliation, most do not meaningfully address urban Indigenous housing needs in their Official Community Plans or housing strategies.

BSH's Comparing First Nations Led Land and Housing Regulation Models across Metro Vancouver project uses cases like Sen̓áḵw to examine how Nations are advancing housing through Indigenous-led land governance, long-term land retention, and regulatory systems that do not depend on municipal zoning frameworks. BSH recommends the related webinar and podcast for additional context.

  • Urban Indigenous housing needs must be identified as distinct needs in local policy rather than folded into general affordability planning
  • Municipal barriers commonly include limited financial and staffing capacity, uncertainty about jurisdiction, and ambiguity about how to respond to Indigenous housing needs
  • First Nations-led housing models retain land, set their own regulatory terms, and align development with cultural and community priorities
  • Sen̓áḵw shows how land retention, rental housing, and Nation-led regulation can support long-term community control in an urban setting
keyPoints: Federal reserve land — exempt from municipal zoning
Project scale: 6,000+ rental homes and 1,200+ below-market homes
Phase One: 1,409 homes across three towers; 250 homes allocated to Indigenous residents through Hiy̓ám̓ Housing
$1.4B in CMHC support for early phases of the project

sections.label: Overview
sections.content:
Granville Island is a federally administered public asset. A 2023 Granville Island Council notice describes it as 15.2 hectares of land plus 2.1 hectares of tidal water, in close proximity to downtown Vancouver.

The same notice states that administration, management, and control were transferred to CMHC by 1973 Order in Council. Granville Island Administration describes the island as operationally self-sustaining, with major revenues from rent and parking.

Granville Island continues to be used as a public policy reference point for how federal public land can support mixed cultural, commercial, and community uses in a high-value urban location.

sections.label: Land Model
sections.content:
The Land Lease Approach

CMHC administers Granville Island on behalf of the Government of Canada and leases space to a diverse tenant mix. Granville Island Administration reports 300+ businesses and 3,000+ jobs, while emphasizing support for arts, culture, and local enterprise.

  • Small businesses and artisans
  • Arts and cultural organizations
  • Free community spaces and public amenities
  • Public Market vendors and food businesses

Economic Profile (2023 Council Notice)

A 2023 Council notice reports Granville Island as generating over $300 million in economic activity, with $105 million in annual sales and about $2 million in annual tax receipts.

Current Challenges

Current Council priorities (2026–2028) identify Financial Sustainability and Asset Management as core focus areas, reflecting ongoing pressure to maintain aging infrastructure while preserving Granville Island's public and cultural role.

Why This Matters for Housing

Granville Island demonstrates key principles relevant to housing policy:

  • Public ownership can prevent land speculation
  • Cross-subsidy can support below-market uses
  • Long-term stewardship requires dedicated asset renewal planning
  • Policy flexibility can enable local innovation

Public Market: 50+ independent food purveyors; island-wide: 300+ businesses and 3,000+ jobs
CMHC administration transferred by 1973 Order in Council; operations described as self-sustaining
2023 Council notice: over $300M economic activity, $105M annual sales, and about $2M tax receipts
